slides.title: Headers: free defence from the server
slides.summary: A handful of HTTP response headers turn on browser protections with no change to your app code.
body: Browsers ship many protections that are off by default for compatibility. Security headers switch them on for your site.
<mark>Set security headers once, at the CDN or server, so every response gets them, including error pages.</mark>

body.note: Check a deployed site in DevTools (Network → a document request → Response headers), or with a public scanner such as Mozilla's HTTP Observatory.

body.text: It's obsolete: browsers removed the XSS auditor it controlled, and the auditor itself could be abused. Omit the header or send 0. CSP replaces it.

viz.title: A good baseline for an app

figure.alt: An HTTP response is shown on the left with seven security headers. Each one points to what it protects against on the right: Content-Security-Policy against XSS and data exfiltration; Strict-Transport-Security against downgrade to HTTP; X-Content-Type-Options nosniff against files run as the wrong type; Referrer-Policy against leaking full URLs to other sites; Permissions-Policy against unwanted camera, microphone or location use; Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy against cross-window attacks and Spectre-style leaks; and frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options against clickjacking.

slides.title: Content Security Policy (CSP)
slides.summary: CSP tells the browser which scripts may run. A strict, nonce-based policy stops injected code even when it reaches the HTML.
body: A CSP is an allowlist for what the page may load and run. Its biggest job is stopping XSS payloads from executing.
Domain allowlists (script-src cdn.example.com) are easy to bypass through JSONP endpoints and old library versions on those domains. A strict CSP uses nonces or hashes instead:

ul: the server puts a fresh random nonce in the header and on each of its own <script> tags;
'strict-dynamic' lets those trusted scripts load further scripts;
injected scripts and inline event handlers have no nonce, so they're blocked.

body: <mark>Roll out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first, fix the reports, then enforce.</mark>

body.more: Static sites and SPAs without a server
body.text: A nonce needs a server to generate it per response. A static build can use hashes of its inline scripts instead ('sha256-…'), which many build tools generate. Angular can add a CSP nonce to its own inline styles and scripts with ngCspNonce or the CSP_NONCE token.
Add Reporting-Endpoints: csp="https://example.com/csp-reports" and report-to csp in the policy. Reports show what would break before you enforce, and reveal attacks after.

steps.caption: Deploy the policy in report-only mode first.

item.label: Fix violations
item.sub: Move inline handlers into code, add nonces

steps.caption: Most reports point at inline scripts and onclick attributes.
Switch to the enforcing header and keep reporting on.
Then lock down DOM sinks as well.

figure.alt: The server generates a random nonce, here r4nd0m, for each response. It sends the header Content-Security-Policy script-src nonce-r4nd0m strict-dynamic and puts nonce="r4nd0m" on its own script tags. In the HTML, the app's own script tag has the nonce and runs; a script it loads is allowed through strict-dynamic. An injected script tag from a comment has no nonce and is blocked, and an inline onerror handler is blocked too. Because the nonce changes on every response, an attacker cannot guess it.

slides.title: Writing CSP directives
slides.summary: Directives say where each type of resource may come from. default-src is the fallback; 'unsafe-inline' undoes most of the protection.
body: Take a news site that serves its own scripts, loads photos from img.newsroom.example, embeds videos from player.videohost.example and sends analytics to collect.metrics.example.

ul: default-src 'self' is the fallback for every resource type you don't list.
Add only what each feature needs: img-src for the photo CDN, frame-src for the video player, connect-src for analytics.
Source keywords: 'self' (your origin), 'none' (nothing), a scheme (https:), a host, 'nonce-…' or 'sha256-…'.

Avoid 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' in script-src: they let injected inline scripts and eval run. When a nonce or hash is present, browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline', which is why it's sometimes kept only as a fallback for very old browsers.
A new nonce for every response; never reuse or hard-code one.
Generated with a cryptographically secure random generator, at least 128 bits, base64-encoded.
Never put untrusted data inside a nonced <script>: the nonce would bless it.
Browsers hide the nonce from the DOM after parsing, so injected code can't read it from the page.

body: <mark>A policy with 'unsafe-inline' in script-src gives almost no XSS protection. Use nonces or hashes instead.</mark>

body.note: Violations appear in the DevTools console with the exact directive that blocked them, e.g. “Refused to load the image … because it violates img-src”. That message tells you which directive to adjust.

figure.alt: default-src sits at the top as the fallback. Under it are fetch directives, each controlling one kind of resource: script-src for JavaScript, style-src for CSS, img-src for images, connect-src for fetch, XHR and WebSockets, font-src for fonts, media-src for audio and video, and frame-src for iframes you embed. If a directive is missing, the browser uses default-src. A second group does not fall back to default-src at all: frame-ancestors (who may frame you), form-action (where forms may submit), base-uri (what the base tag may be) and upgrade-insecure-requests. Example: with default-src self and img-src self https://images.example, images may come from the image CDN, but a script from that CDN is still blocked because script-src falls back to default-src self.

slides.title: HSTS, nosniff, Referrer-Policy and COOP
slides.summary: The other headers each close one specific gap. Most are one line.

ul: Strict-Transport-Security makes the browser use HTTPS for your domain for max-age seconds, even if the user types http://.
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops the browser guessing a file's type, so an uploaded “image” can't run as a script.
Referrer-Policy controls how much of the URL is sent to other sites. URLs often contain IDs and tokens.
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin cuts the link between your window and cross-origin pages it opens or is opened by. Use same-origin-allow-popups if you rely on OAuth or payment popups.

body.text: Adding Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp (or credentialless) to COOP makes the page cross-origin isolated. That unlocks SharedArrayBuffer and precise timers, which are otherwise restricted because of Spectre-style attacks.
